fast.topic: The Monday fast hour covers Week 2 of Nigerian Peoples and Culture, Dr Abimbola Oyarinu's lecture on intergroup relations among pre-colonial Nigerian peoples. It opens with the definition of inter-group relations as interaction between two or more distinct linguistic and cultural groups, the two identifiers of a group (culture and language), and the scale of Nigerian diversity - over 348 language groups and 374 ethnic groups. The bulk of the hour works through the four indicators used to reconstruct pre-colonial interaction. Traditions of origin covers the shared Kanuri and Hausa myths tracing to Baghdad through Saif and Bayajidda, Bayajidda settling among the Kanuri and marrying the Mai's daughter, the Kisra legend founding the Yoruba and Borgu kingdoms with the Ooni of Ife as Kisra's brother, the Yoruba-Benin link through Oranmiyan and Eweka, and the Umu-Ezechinma Igbo and Isoko ties to Edo. Conflict covers the Oyo-Nupe wars and the Bariba-Yoruba alliance, the Kano-Katsina wars over trade routes, Jukun conquest over the Kanuri, Hausa, Igala, Idoma and Ebira, Benin's expansion to Auchi, Idah, Itsekiri, Urhobo, Isoko, Okpe and Eko (Lagos) with the Benin-descended Lagos kings Ado and Asipa, and the Igala-Nsukka Igbo wars that left the Illah speaking Igbo while their masquerades speak Igala. Trade and commerce covers the Jukun salt-for-Tiv-firewood exchange, Kanem-Bornu's role in the trans-Saharan trade as the channel for Yoruba and Nupe participation, Ibibio land as the corridor between hinterland Igbo and coastal Efik and Ijaw, and Nupe goods traded to the Yoruba. Religion covers shared indigenous practices and borrowed deities and cults: Yoruba Igunu from Nupe Ndakogbaya, Ibibio-origin Ibini Ukpabi among the Igbo, Efik-origin Ekpe and Ekpo among Igbo subgroups, and the Bori cult across Hausaland. The hour closes with Nigeria's six geo-political zones and their dominant ethnic groups, and Nigeria's history dating back to 39,000 BC.

deep.topic: Conceptual session on Week 2 exactly as Dr Adeniji builds it: Coulomb's law F = k|q₁q₂|/r² as a magnitude-only law for a pair of point charges with k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N m²/C²; why a third charge forces the separate principle of superposition of forces, and what 'vector sum' means on a line; her subscript convention Fᵢⱼ; the definition E = F/q₀ in N/C with a positive unit test charge, and |E| = k|Q|/r² as Coulomb's law with the test charge divided out; radially outward from +Q and radially inward toward −Q; the field-line rules; and F = qE, so that the force on an electron is antiparallel to E.

fast.topic: The Tuesday fast hour covers Week 2 of Introduction to Web Technologies, which is a protocol-and-markup survey rather than a coding week. It opens with the four transfer protocols the week is titled after - HTTP as the insecure foundation of web data communication, HTTPS as its encrypted counterpart, FTP as the unencrypted file transfer protocol, and SFTP as the secure extension that adds encryption and strong authentication. It then moves to markup languages as the backbone of structured content: HTML for structuring web content through elements, tags and attributes; XML for storing and exchanging structured data using user-defined tags; SVG for scalable two-dimensional vector graphics; MathML for mathematical notation; and XHTML as HTML reformulated as an XML application. The email block follows, splitting SMTP (sending and relaying outgoing mail, with its HELO, MAIL FROM and RCPT TO commands) from the retrieval protocols POP3 (downloads for offline access) and IMAP (keeps mail on the server and synchronises across devices), plus MIME for non-ASCII text and attachments. Next comes the Domain Name System: domain name resolution, name-to-IP mapping and reverse lookup, the root domain, TLD, second-level domain and subdomain hierarchy, resolvers and authoritative servers, MX records, and DNSSEC for signing DNS data against cache poisoning. The hour closes on web communication protocols - WebSocket's full-duplex persistent TCP connection, REST's stateless resource-based use of GET, POST, PUT and DELETE mapped to CRUD, and SOAP's strict XML messaging - with their stated advantages and disadvantages. The emphasis throughout is memorising acronym expansions and being able to discriminate each pair, since that is what the assessment format rewards.

deep.topic: The Wednesday deep hour takes Week 2's material conceptually, without traces or arithmetic. It starts from the lesson's own definition of a problem-solving strategy - a plan, made of multiple steps, used to find a solution or overcome a challenge - and the claim that different problems require different strategies, so that choosing and then studying a strategy's rules and procedures is part of solving rather than a delay. It then works through the internal mechanism of each of the six named strategies: brainstorming's dependence on volume of ideas and on deferred criticism; the heuristic trade of rationality for speed, valid only where a sub-optimal solution is acceptable; trial-and-error's cost scaling with the number of candidate solutions; means-ends analysis fixing the intended solution in advance and decomposing the problem so each part gets its best-suited approach; abstraction deleting the attributes that will not help reach a solution and leaving a model; and analogy transferring understanding from a known system, valid only while the underlying principles are the same. For each, the session asks what it costs and under what conditions it fails. The second half covers the conceptual basis of the week's classifications: well-defined versus ill-defined, and routine versus non-routine as a question of whether a standard method exists rather than whether arithmetic is involved. It closes on solvability - what the universal Turing machine contributes to the idea of an algorithm, and why "unsolvable" is a claim about the absence of a systematic decision procedure for every input rather than a claim that no answer exists, with decidable and undecidable problems and the halting problem treated in those terms.

fast.topic: The Wednesday fast hour covers GST_122 Week 2, "Communication and Meaning", whose organising claim is that the ultimate goal of communication is that meaning is conveyed accurately, and that communication is not solely about words. Start with semiotics - the field of signs and symbols and the role they play in everyday interaction - and the point that meaning travels through non-verbal signs as well as language. Then drill the central distinction the course examines on: denotative meaning (the literal, dictionary sense) versus connotative meaning (the implied or suggested sense, carrying cultural and emotional associations), practising on example words rather than reciting the definitions. Next take the two named sources of confusion, hazardous homophones and ambiguity, and learn the discriminating test between them: written down, a homophone problem disappears while an ambiguous sentence is still readable two ways. Work through the week's case study, "The Ambiguity Challenge in Project Coordination", in which a single ambiguous task-assignment sentence produced conflicting interpretations of tasks and responsibilities across a project team. Close by memorising the lesson's definition of effective communication - conveying intended meanings accurately while being mindful of the broader cultural and emotional associations of words - and the six named competencies: Semiotic Awareness, Contextual Interpretation, Clarity in Expression, Active Listening, Conflict Resolution and Cultural Sensitivity. Since the course tests classification of examples, spend the last ten minutes labelling sample sentences as denotative, connotative, homophone or ambiguity.

deep.topic: This session works the same Week 2 function material as problems: reading a question, choosing a method, executing it accurately and checking the result. It covers evaluating compositions in the correct order and seeing that f o g and g o f differ; finding the largest domain of an expression that combines a logarithm with a denominator, where two separate restrictions must both be imposed; completing the square on a quadratic to locate its vertex, axis of symmetry and direction of opening; solving an absolute-value equation by splitting it into its two cases; solving an exponential equation by isolating the power and recognising it as a power of the base; evaluating a piecewise function at and either side of its boundary point by first deciding which condition the input satisfies; recovering a line's equation from two points via the slope formula and point-slope form; and solving a logarithmic equation by combining logs, clearing the log, and then rejecting the root that violates the domain. The written questions are diagnostic: naming exactly where standard wrong routes go astray - squaring an absolute-value equation and manufacturing extraneous roots, treating 5^x as 5 times x, taking c to be the vertex y-coordinate - and checking a vertex by independent means before reading end behaviour off a cubic.

fast.topic: The Thursday fast hour covers Week 2 of General Physics Practical II: Ohmic resistance and the experiment to verify Ohm's law. Start with the statement of Ohm's law - current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it at constant temperature - and the equation V = IR with each symbol and unit defined, plus the distinction between ohmic resistors (constant R, straight V-I line through the origin, reversible behaviour) and non-ohmic ones such as varistors, photoresistors and thermistors. Then drill the two combination rules: series resistors carry the same current and add as R = R1 + R2 + ... + RN, while parallel resistors share the same potential difference and combine as 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ..., checked against the worked values 10 ohm, 20 ohm and 30 ohm giving 60 ohm in series and 5.45 ohm in parallel. Next walk the Praxilabs virtual Ohmic Resistor procedure in order: wire the breadboard circuit, connect the voltmeter in parallel and the ammeter in series, connect the DC power supply, set R1 between 1 and 20 kilohm, apply a chosen voltage with the knob or slider, press Record, and repeat six more times for seven data points before the Excel file downloads. Finish on the analysis that carries the marks: plot V on the y-axis against I in mA on the x-axis, map V = IR onto y = mx + c so that the gradient is the resistance and a zero intercept confirms no systematic offset, watch the unit trap that volts per milliamp gives kilohms, and compute the percentage error against the 1 kilohm default value, which must fall within 5 per cent for the verification to pass.

deep.topic: Problems-only session on Week 2. deep.topic: The Saturday session is COS_102 applied, working the week's method through on concrete cases rather than restating it. The student is given stated problems and has to classify them by testing rather than by surface appearance - recognising that Bridget's 50-question exam-marks problem is non-routine despite using only arithmetic, that the parking-space area is routine because a known formula applies, and that "approximate the number of hairs on your head" is non-routine rather than unsolvable. Scenarios are then read and matched to the strategy actually in use, including cases designed to mislead: XYZ Corporation's $2bn turnover target decomposed into quarterly and regional targets is means-ends analysis, while the doctor converging several weaker rays on a deep tumour after recalling an army dividing to take a fortress is analogy, not means-ends, despite the division into smaller parts. The session runs the two ordered procedures of the week in sequence - the three analogy steps and the three steps for attacking a non-routine problem. It traces the substitution puzzle one replacement at a time, obtaining BOOOB from BOB via the rules OB->BOOB and BOB->O. Finally it diagnoses attempts that went wrong: a heuristic applied to a routine problem where an exact answer is required, a brainstorming session ruined by immediate criticism, and a premature conclusion that a substitution puzzle does not come out. The halting problem is met applied, as a request to write a program that decides termination for any input.

questions.q: The definition of a function f: A → B says every element of A is assigned **exactly one** element of B. If "exactly one" were weakened to "at least one", what specifically breaks?
options: The domain would no longer be the whole of A.
The symbol f(x) would no longer name a definite value.
The range could become larger than the codomain.
The function could no longer be surjective.
questions.concept: The uniqueness clause in the definition of a function
questions.why: Weakening 'exactly one' to 'at least one' lets a single input carry two outputs, so the notation f(x) no longer denotes a single definite value.

questions.q: The vertical line test detects the failure of which clause?
options: That the domain is an unbroken interval.
That every element of the codomain is used.
That no two inputs share an output.
That each input has only one output.
questions.concept: What the vertical line test actually tests
questions.why: A vertical line collects every point with the same first coordinate, so two intersections mean one input has two outputs - a failure of uniqueness of output, not of injectivity or surjectivity.

questions.q: A map f: A → B is described as surjective but not injective. Which must be true?
options: Every element of B is reached, and some element of B twice.
Every element of A is reached, and some element of A twice.
The range is a proper subset of the codomain of f.
f has a well-defined inverse on the whole of B.
questions.concept: Distinguishing surjective from injective
questions.why: Surjective means every element of the codomain is reached; not injective means some element of the codomain is reached by more than one input.

questions.q: f: A → B is surjective but fails to be injective. What exactly goes wrong when you try to define f⁻¹?
options: f⁻¹ would have a domain larger than B.
f⁻¹ would be undefined at some elements of B.
Some element of B would have to be sent to two different elements of A.
f⁻¹ ∘ f would be the identity on B instead of on A.
questions.concept: Why invertibility requires injectivity
questions.why: If two inputs share an output, the proposed inverse would have to send that one output to two different inputs, which is not a function.

questions.q: log_b(x) is defined only for b > 0 **and b ≠ 1**. What is the reason for excluding b = 1?
options: A power of the number 1 has no defined value at all.
log₁(x) would come out negative whenever x is below 1.
The curve y = 1^x would fail to cross the y-axis anywhere.
Every power of 1 equals 1, so nothing else is reachable.
questions.concept: Why the logarithm base excludes b = 1
questions.why: Since 1^y = 1 for every y, the function 1^x is constant and hits no other value, so it has no inverse to serve as log base 1.

questions.q: In f(x) = 2x + 1 for x ≤ 0 and f(x) = x² − 3 for x > 0, why is the second condition written x > 0 rather than x ≥ 0?
options: Because x = 0 is already assigned by the first branch.
Because the expression x² − 3 has no defined value when x is 0.
Because the two branches are required to agree in value at x = 0.
Because the graph of a function must be unbroken at a boundary.
questions.concept: Why piecewise conditions must be disjoint
questions.why: x = 0 is already covered by x <= 0; using x >= 0 in the second branch would assign x = 0 both 1 and -3, destroying single-valuedness.

questions.q: Why is |x| defined by two cases (x if x ≥ 0, −x if x < 0) instead of the instruction "remove the minus sign"?
options: Because −x is a positive number whatever the value of x.
Because the graph of |x| has to be smooth at the origin.
Because which case applies depends on x, not on a visible sign.
Because absolute value is defined for real inputs only.
questions.concept: Why absolute value is defined by cases
questions.why: The rule cannot be 'remove the minus sign' because in |x - 3| there is no visible sign - which case applies is determined by the value of x.

questions.q: For a polynomial of degree n with leading coefficient aₙ, why do those two numbers alone decide the shape of the graph far from the origin?
options: Because the lower-degree terms become zero once |x| is large.
Because every other term, divided by aₙxⁿ, tends to 0 as |x| grows.
Because polynomials of equal degree have identical graphs.
Because a₀ is only the y-intercept and never affects shape.
questions.concept: Why degree and leading coefficient fix end behaviour
questions.why: Dividing any lower-degree term by the leading term gives a ratio tending to 0 as |x| grows, so the leading term dominates - the other terms become negligible relative to it, not zero in themselves.

questions.q: Every function is a relation, but not every relation is a function. Explain the difference using the slide's set language — "A has many B" versus "B can have many A" — and say which of those two situations is allowed.
questions.concept: Every function is a relation; the converse fails on the uniqueness clause
questions.why: A relation is any pairing of elements of A with elements of B. A function is a relation with one extra restriction: each element of A is paired with exactly one element of B. In the slide's language, 'B can have many A' is allowed - several different inputs may share one output, which is just a many-to-one function. What is forbidden is 'A has many B': one input carrying several outputs. That is the situation the vertical line test detects, and it is precisely what stops a relation from being a function.

questions.q: The vertical line test and the horizontal line test look almost identical but answer different questions. Explain what property each one is testing and why a graph can pass one and fail the other.
questions.concept: The two line tests check different clauses of the pairing
questions.why: The vertical line test checks whether each input has only one output - that is, whether the relation is a function at all. The horizontal line test checks whether each output comes from only one input - that is, whether the function is injective and therefore invertible. A graph can pass the first and fail the second: y = x^2 is a perfectly good function, since every x gives exactly one y, but the line y = 4 meets it twice, so two inputs share an output and it has no inverse on R. The two tests scan in perpendicular directions because they interrogate opposite halves of the pairing.

questions.q: Explain why f(x) = b^x and g(x) = log_b(x) are called inverses, and why the domain of one is the range of the other. Use this to explain why log_b(x) is undefined for x ≤ 0.
questions.concept: Exponential and logarithm as mutual inverses, with domain and range exchanged
questions.why: log_b(x) is defined as the exponent to which b must be raised to give x, so b^(log_b x) = x and log_b(b^x) = x - each undoes the other, which is exactly what makes them inverses. Under inversion the domain and range swap: b^x has domain all reals and range (0, inf), so log_b(x) has domain (0, inf) and range all reals. That is why log_b(x) is undefined for x <= 0 - no real exponent applied to a positive base ever produces zero or a negative number, so there is nothing for the logarithm to return.

questions.q: A slide states that in f(x) = ax² + bx + c, "c is the y-coordinate of the vertex". Explain why this is false as written, what c genuinely is, and the one special case in which the slide's claim happens to be true.
questions.concept: What c actually is in ax^2 + bx + c, and the single case where the slide is accidentally right
questions.why: c is the y-intercept: setting x = 0 gives f(0) = c, so c is the height at which the curve crosses the y-axis. The vertex sits at x = -b/(2a), and its y-coordinate is f(-b/(2a)) = c - b^2/(4a), which differs from c by b^2/(4a). The slide's claim is therefore false whenever b is not zero. The one special case in which it happens to be true is b = 0: the vertex then lies on the y-axis at x = 0, so the vertex's y-coordinate and the y-intercept are the same point, and both equal c.
